extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent agents, examiners and legal practitioners dealing with UK patents under the Patents, Designs, and Trade Marks Act 1883
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing and prosecuting a patent application (provisional and complete specifications, drawings, titles, claims, examiner/comptroller interaction, time limits and appeals) under the 1883 Act in the UK. Focuses on what must be disclosed and procedural requirements to obtain and defend a valid patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to apply / who may apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person (including British subjects, two or more persons jointly, bodies corporate, women, infants, and personal representatives of deceased inventors) may make an application for a patent; the applicant must be the first and true inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint applications may be made and a declaration attached may be taken by one or more applicants. A body corporate may be registered as proprietor by its corporate name (Patents Rules). If the applicant is not the first and true inventor the patent, if granted, will be void. (References: sect. 4(1)-(2); s.117; cases noted in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and language of application
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must be made in the prescribed form (First Schedule/Patents Forms) and in the English language, and must be left at or sent to the Patent Office in the prescribed manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New forms are prescribed by Patents Rules; the formal application form (Forms A, A1) must contain the required declaration. Stamped forms and where to obtain them are set out in Patents Instructions. Delivery by post counts as the ordinary delivery time (s.97; Patents Rules, 19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration requirement in application
rubrics_metrics.description: An application must contain a declaration that the applicant is in possession of an invention and that he (or one or more joint applicants) claims to be the true and first inventor and desires to obtain a patent; the application must be accompanied by either a provisional or a complete specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The declaration must be signed (see rules re: statutory declarations if made abroad or before certain officers). Failure to include the declaration or required specification will render the application defective. (Sect. 5 sub-s. (2), statutes and Patents Forms cross-referenced.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional specification content
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional specification must describe the nature of the invention; it need not contain all minute directions or enable a workman of ordinary skill fully to make the invention, but must disclose what the invention really is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional spec must commence with a title; a claim is not necessary. It suffices if it shows the invention in a rough state (cases: Stoner v. Todd; Bailey v. Roberton; In re Newall and Elliott). Provisional spec requires no stamp. Drawings should accompany when required. Omitting essential information can be fatal later when comparing with the complete specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete specification core requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete specification must particularly describe and ascertain the nature of the invention and in what manner it is to be performed; it must begin with a title and end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete spec must be supplemental to any provisional spec and should not go beyond or vary from the nature of the invention disclosed in the provisional. It requires a stamp. Failure to describe the invention particularly or to state how to perform it can render the patent void. (See sect. 5 and attendant notes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Title requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The title must disclose the object of the invention and must not describe the invention in wider terms than are found in the remainder of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the title is wider than the specification the patent may be void (cases cited). The examiner is to report whether the title sufficiently indicates the subject-matter of the invention; title can be used to narrow claims. The comptroller may require amendment of the title. (Examples: R. v. Else; Newton v. Vaucher; Patents Rules references.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim requirement and relation to title
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete specification must end with a distinct statement (claim) of the invention claimed; the claim ought not to exceed the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically claims were used mainly to disclaim old matter, but under the Act the complete specification must include a distinct claim. Overly broad claims exceeding the title risk invalidity. The claim should properly delimit what is new and claimed as the inventor's invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency: intelligibility to skilled workman
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be intelligible to ordinary workmen in the trade or business to which the invention is applicable, possessing some knowledge of the trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification fails to enable a workman of ordinary skill to carry out the invention (e.g., omits material parts or essential directions), the patent may be held void. Cases and examples illustrate failures of intelligibility and their consequences (Neilson v. Harford; The Hounsehill Co. v. Nellsoriy).

rubrics_metrics.name: No omission of material parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must not omit any material part of the process or apparatus necessary for carrying the invention into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omissions such as failing to state a required reagent, how a solution is to be applied, or that heat is necessary have led to patents being void (e.g., Liardet v. Johnson; Wood v. Zimmer; Bailey v. Roberton). Where material parts are omitted the specification is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: No misleading representations in material particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must not contain misleading representations in any material particular (e.g., asserting certain materials will work when they will not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misleading statements about suitable materials, essential/unessential ingredients, or material forms have been held fatal (Turner v. Winter; Crompton v. Ibbotson; Wegmann v. Corcoran; Lewis v. Marling). Be accurate about capabilities and essential components.

rubrics_metrics.name: No ambiguous statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must avoid ambiguity (for example as to proportions of ingredients or the nature/uncertainty of materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguities (e.g., proportion statements) can render a specification insufficient, though stating the best proportions is acceptable; generic phrases such as 'or other suitable material' have been construed in case law (Muniz v. Foster; Patent Type Founding Co. v. Richards; Ralston v. Smith). Use clarity in numeric/operational details where material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish new from old (novelty in specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should, where necessary, carefully distinguish what is new from what is old; otherwise the patent may be held to claim what is old and be void for want of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies especially to improvements on existing patents and machines; old matter should be disclaimed (usually in the claim). Incidental references to universally known old things need not be treated as part of the invention. Methods of disclaiming old matter (claims, drawings) discussed in cases (Crane v. Price; Netvall v. Elliott; Daw v. Eley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of best method / most beneficial mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete specification must disclose the most beneficial (best) way known to the patentee for exercising the invention; failure to do so can render the patent void as a fraud on the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee omits material methods actually used in practice or conceals cheaper methods, the patent can be void (Wood v. Zimmer; Turner v. Winter; Savory v. Price). All improvements or discoveries known up to lodging the complete specification should be disclosed (Crossley v. Beverley).

rubrics_metrics.name: No material variation between provisional and complete specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete specification ought not to vary materially from the provisional specification so as to claim a different invention; substantial variation may invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner compares provisional and complete specs to ascertain substantial identity; favourable examiner report is not conclusive and courts may still consider variation (Bailey v. Roherton; Penn v. Bibby; Thomas v. Welch). Parts of provisional may be omitted in the complete spec if there is no fraud and the remaining effect is not altered (Thomas v. Welch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings required when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications (provisional or complete) must be accompanied by drawings when required — i.e., whenever without drawings a workman of ordinary skill could not carry out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings may also serve to explain ambiguities or to restrict an otherwise overly general specification (Hastings v. Brown; Daw v. Eley). Absence of a scale can be an imperfection; drawings must enable a competent workman to make the machine or carry out the invention (Bovill v. Moore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings format and copy rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must conform to prescribed sizes and formats (half sheets or imperial drawing paper within specified borders), no colour, Indian black ink lines; a copy on rolled imperial drawing paper or thin Bristol board of same size must also be left, delivered flat or rolled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sizes given: 19 x 12 inches or 27 x 19 inches with half-inch margins (Patents Rules, 28; Instructions, 12). If application accepted, applicant must furnish a drawing illustrating features of novelty not more than 16 inches square accompanied by a concise explanatory statement (Patents Rules, 28–29; Instructions, 13). No colour; all lines in Indian black ink.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's report: scope and criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must report whether (1) the nature of the invention has been fairly described, (2) the application/specification/drawings have been prepared in the prescribed manner, and (3) the title sufficiently indicates the subject-matter of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner's report is not published or open to public inspection and is not conclusive, though courts are likely to be reluctant to upset a patent where the examiner reported favourably. The report may be produced in appeals to the law officer or where courts certify production desirable in interests of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller's power to require amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner reports deficiencies (e.g., nature not fairly described, documents not prepared in prescribed manner, title insufficient), the comptroller may require the application, specification or drawings to be amended before proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before requiring amendment the comptroller must give 14 days' notice to the applicant; the applicant may request to be heard and may submit written statements or attend personally. The comptroller may not arbitrarily refuse without giving opportunity to amend; refusal is subject to appeal to the law officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedure to the law officer
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may appeal the comptroller's requirement or refusal to the law officer within prescribed time (generally fourteen days); the law officer may hear parties, admit further evidence, and make orders about acceptance subject to conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice of appeal must be filed in Form T; the comptroller transmits papers to the law officer's clerk, who gives seven days' notice of hearing (special leave may shorten notice). Evidence used at hearing is the same as before the comptroller, but new matters may be admitted; witnesses who made affidavits may be ordered to attend for cross-examination; costs may be ordered and enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit to file complete specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If a complete specification is not left with the application, the applicant may leave it within nine months from the date of application; if a complete specification is not left within that time the application is deemed abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving a complete specification with the application gives immediate protection under s.15 but has disadvantages (forecloses further experiments and risks losing additional fee if refused). Provisional specification abandoned under these rules is not published until acceptance of a complete specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for acceptance and effect of non-acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless a complete specification is accepted within twelve months from the date of application (save where an appeal is pending), the application becomes void at the expiration of those twelve months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner compares provisional and complete specifications and reports; failure to obtain acceptance within 12 months (subject to allowable appeals) causes the application to lapse. Obtaining provisional protection and later acceptance have different legal effects (see sects. 14 and 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and sealing date / publication timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Lodging the application gives the applicant priority over later applicants for the same invention, and a patent if granted is sealed as of the day of application; no infringement action lies for acts done before publication of the complete specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of an application accompanied by a provisional specification gives provisional protection under s.14 (enables use and publication without prejudicing grant, but infringement action may not be maintainable until grant/conditions). Acceptance of a complete specification results in immediate publication and inspection rights as per rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling competing/similar applications
rubrics_metrics.description: If a later application bearing the same or a similar title appears, the examiner must report if it comprises the same invention; the comptroller may, subject to appeal, refuse to seal a patent to the second applicant if the inventions are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both applicants must be given opportunity to be heard before the comptroller decides. Prior applicants are further protected by opposition on advertisement of the complete specification and under sect.13 (sealing of the patent to a prior applicant may still be possible even if the later applicant obtains sealing). Titles may be amended to reveal similarity; examiner's report on title helps detect identity.
